Flying 250 miles above the Earth, the International Space Station (ISS) 
provides a platform for research to improve life on Earth, enable space 
exploration, and understand the universe. This Researcher’s Guide is 
intended to help potential ISS combustion science researchers plan 
experiments utilizing the microgravity environment in order to understand 
how heat and mass transport phenomena coupled with chemistry affect 
combustion behavior and fire safety. It covers the nature of the acceleration 
environment on ISS, available facilities for conducting combustion research, 
examples of previous microgravity investigations, and current combustion 
science and fire safety projects being developed for execution on the ISS.

Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) 
 
 
Abstract 
 
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Re-flight (SAMER) is an extension or continuation of Smoke Aerosol 
Measurement Experiment (SAME), conducted in space from September 9 to October 5, 2007. On the success of 
SAME, SAMER included the following modifications: 1) a new test sample material Pyrell®, an intumescent fire-
retardant foam by Foamex was introduced to replace DBP samples, 2) test condition ranges was extended to include 
higher heating temperature and no-flow conditions, and 3) a new instrument, M-pass, developed in-house GRC, was 
used to replace one of the two Commercial Diagnostic Enclosures used in SAME. SAMER flight tests were 
conducted from July 16, to September 9, 2010, successfully completing 66 test points. As a part of SAMER effort, 
three major post–flight ground tests were performed: the SAMER apparatus flow tests to obtain accurate dilution 
ratio data, the TEM tests to obtain the 1-g counterpart of TEM samples and a batch of SMPS tests to examine the 
validity of the lognormal distribution assumption of aerosol particle size for the tested materials. Based on the 
results of both SAMER flight and ground-based tests, it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the 
lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective approach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in 
space vehicles. Particle size distributions of aerosol produced from 5 tested materials commonly found in space 
crafts were identified.

Abstract 
 
Leaks, fires, and spills are some of the most significant hazards that must be accounted for in the 
design of the environmental control and life-support system on spacecraft. While prevention is 
certainly the first line of defense against a fire, early detection of a overheat event or an actual 
fire allows the crew to respond before the hazard gets out of control. The limited options 
available for response to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an 
earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications.  This report describes 
the outcomes of the Smoke Aerosol Measurements Experiment (SAME), an experiment 
conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the International Space Station (ISS) 
to characterize the size distribution of smoke particulate produced in low-gravity from a variety 
of overheated spacecraft materials The absence of gravity can impact not only the formation of 
the smoke particulate but also the aging and coagulation processes that occur as the particulate 
are transported from their source to a detector. 
 
Based on the results of an earlier flight project carried out in the Glovebox of the Space Shuttle, 
(Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD)), the soot particles generated and observed in low gravity 
environment tend to be larger in size than those in earth conditions. However, the preliminary 
results of CSD project were not conclusive because of a minor variation of the temperature of hot 
wire which heated the test sample to generate smoke, and also because the CSD apparatus could 
not measure the liquid drops existing in the smoke produced by several of the samples. 
Furthermore, the CSD project was not designed to provide on-orbit measurement of the particle 
size distribution. The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment was designed to obtain this data 
that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration 
missions. Unfortunately, because of the relatively small volume of the MSG, it cannot 
accommodate the instruments normally used in a ground-based laboratory to measure the size 
distribution of smoke particulate. Therefore, a new procedure was developed, the moment 
method, from which the characteristics of the particle size distribution can be inferred using a 
minimum number of portable instrument.

Smoke points were measured in microgravity aboard the International Space Station 
(ISS) as part of the Smoke Points in Coflow Experiment (SPICE), and in normal 
gravity conditions. In microgravity conditions increasing the coflow velocity or 
decreasing the burner diameter increased the smoke point flame length. A simplified 
prediction of centerline jet velocity did not yield residence-time-based criticalities or 
data collapse. Simulation of non-reacting flows showed that the simplified centerline 
velocity prediction was able to predict velocity decay for only relatively weak 
coflows. An improved model may yield different results. In normal earth gravity 
coflow velocity exhibited mixed effects. For burner diameters of 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 
mm, smoke points increased with increases of coflow velocity. For an unconfined 
coflow burner with a burner diameter of 13.7 mm smoke point length decreased with 
increasing coflow velocity for ethylene and propylene, while increasing for propane 
flames.

I.  
Introduction 
 
A. 
Hypothesis 
The hypothesis of the SPICE investigation is that smoke point behavior 
will be observed for co-flowing flames and that it will show 
dependence on nozzle diameter and coflow velocity. 
 
B. 
Objectives of Investigation 
The objective of the SPICE experiment is to find the laminar smoke-point 
properties of nonbuoyant jet diffusion flames (i.e., the properties of the 
largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot) for several fuels 
under different nozzle diameter/ co-flow velocity configurations.  
Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify 
models of the flame shapes under co-flow conditions.  
 
C. 
Previous Mission Experience 
 
N/A 
 
D. 
Background/History of Project (Optional) 
 
The SPICE experiment was an outgrowth of the Laminar Soot Processes 
Experiment (LSP) which flew on STS 83, 94, and 107.  SPICE utilized the 
design heritage and modified the hardware from the Enclosed Laminar Flames 
Experiment (ELF) which flew in the Middeck Glovebox on STS 87. 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
 
A. 
Discussion of Method/Protocol 
 
Most tests were conducted by setting the coflow velocity, igniting the flame, 
and adjusting the fuel flow rate. Approximate smoke points were identified in 
the video by the flight crew and simultaneously by the ground support crew in 
Cleveland. Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the 
MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air.  After the tests the video 
record was analyzed to identify smoke point conditions. The associated 
coflow and fuel flow rates were obtained from digital data recorded in the 
video. The smoke point lengths, LSP, were obtained from the video record 
and are the measured distance from the burner tip to the tip of the luminous 
flame on the flame axis.

III. Results 
 
A. 
List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
 
SPICE operated very successfully with the only significant anomaly being the 
accumulation of soot in the outlet screen which changed the flow behavior in 
the duct.  This was corrected by a crew member using the vacuum to clean the 
outlet screen on June 15. 
B. 
Completeness/Quality of Data 
During Increment 18 SPICE conducted 108 test points completing its nominal 
test matrix. During Increments 19/20 SPICE conducted 155 additional test 
points the provided improved resolution of the smoke points and allowed us to 
explore further limits in the parameter space. 
C. Status of Data Analysis:  The data from the down linked video have been analyzed 
for flame length and smoke point flow rate.  These have resulted in a meeting apper 
and a draft journal paper.  More work will be conducted with analysis of the digital 
luminance data from the Nikon.

Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) 
Abstract 
The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins 
to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal 
gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels. 
Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss 
fractions of turbulent diffusion flames.  SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in non-
buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co-flowing air aboard the International Space Station. 
Fifty-two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen 
mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 
65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, 
burner diameter, and co-flow velocity. Increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame 
lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. 
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co-flowing flames. These trends can be explained 
qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally 
correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they 
increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The measured smoke point lengths were found to 
correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The 
measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion 
flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of 
residence times in coflowing flames is developed, and although residence time helps explain 
many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements 
yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames.

the astronauts that conducted the tests (M. Barratt, E.M. Fincke, S.H. Magnus, and K. Wakata). 
The SPICE project was conducted through the ISS Exploration Research Project of the

I.  Introduction 
The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is conducted 
in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, an 
electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner and a flat, 
circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.  The motion of the 
charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong 
electric field.  The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting 
behavior of the flame.  Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing 
through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and 
stability.  Conducting the tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis of 
ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the development 
of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. 
 
An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a 
result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the 
soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer.  The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames

NASA Glenn Provides the Keys With the Fluids 
and Combustion Facility
What Is Microgravity?
	
Gravity is a force that governs motion 
throughout the universe. It holds us to the 
ground and keeps the Earth in orbit around the 
Sun. Microgravity describes the environment 
in orbital space flight, which has very weak 
gravitational effects (one-millionth of what is 
felt on Earth) and which is sometimes referred 
to as a state of “weightlessness.” The condition 
of microgravity occurs when an object is in 
“free fall.” In free fall, an object falls faster and 
faster, accelerating with exactly the speed of 
attraction caused by gravity. Objects travelling 
around the Earth in a state of continuous free 
fall, or orbit, are essentially weightless even 
though their mass remains the same.
	
Conducting research in a microgravity 
environment gives researchers a unique oppor­
tunity to study the true nature of processes and 
materials without having to consider the effects 
of Earth’s gravity. Thus, physics theories can be 
tested at levels of accuracy that are impossible 
on Earth. Microgravity experiments uncover the 
mystery of how gravity affects processes such 
as combustion science and fluid physics. This 
knowledge can then help to improve the way 
we do things on Earth.
Astronaut Michael Fincke, Expedition 18 commander, works on the Combustion Integrated Rack in the Destiny 
Laboratory of the International Space Station.

A World-Class Orbiting Laboratory
	
The term “microgravity” will become more com­
monplace when the International Space Station (ISS) is 
fully operational. The ISS will be the largest orbiting space 
structure and the largest international scientific and tech­
nological endeavor in history. Sixteen countries, including 
the United States, are participating in this record-breaking 
project. The ISS is a permanent laboratory in space where 
studies can be performed without the effects of gravity.
	
The space station provides researchers with all the 
laboratory space and equipment and electrical power 
needed for safe, long-term research by human beings in 
space. The ISS enables larger and longer experiments than 
were possible on the typical 2-week space shuttle mission. 
This gives scientists time for more detailed observation in 
the microgravity environment.
	
The knowledge gained from ISS microgravity experi­
ments is benefiting research on Earth in many fields. Our 
understanding of theories relevant to everything from high-
temperature superconductivity to weather prediction will 
be advanced. New insights into areas such as human health 
and disease prevention and treatment will be achieved. In 
addition, scientists are using the microgravity environment 
to uncover other, more subtle forces and interactions in flu­
ids and materials. By essentially taking gravitational effects 
out of the equation, researchers are able to study as primary 
characteristics what would have been secondary behaviors 
on Earth.
	
Simple investigations of fluid interfaces and combus­
tion processes can be addressed in small, contained experi­
ments, such as the shuttle Glovebox experiments. However, 
more complex and challenging investigations require dedi­
cated facilities to contain fluids and products of combustion 
in a controlled and safe environment.
The ISS Fluids and Combustion Facility
	
The United States Laboratory Module on the ISS con­

challenges of working with fluids and combustion pro­

capabilities comparable to those found in traditional Earth-

1.  Overview 
The CFI experiments are conceived as follow-up experiments to the FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments 
onboard the ISS to further explore the newly discovered quasi-steady “cool flames.”  Cool flames are controlled by low 
temperature chemistry, and occur in the NTC region of n-alkane fuels.  FLEX series of experiments showed for the first 
time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, 
without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature 
is higher than 1200 K.  Since the cool-flame chemistry depends on the chemical structure of the fuel as well as pressure 
and temperature, three different fuel combinations were investigated, namely, pure n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-
dodecane mixtures and farnesane ( a renewable jet fuel) at ambient pressures up to 5 atmospheres. Cool flame 
extinction occurs when its static stability is lost close to the lower turnover point in the NTC region, addition of helium to 
the ambient gas is also considered. Results for droplet burning rates, flame dynamics, droplet extinction diameters, and 
flame radiant out put are measured. 
 
2.  Introduction (PS):  
Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental importance. 
The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day which averages out to an 
astonishing 2.5 gallons per day per person (Reitz, 2013). The primary reasons for such a high reliance on hydrocarbon 
fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but globally, is their high energy density, ease of 
handling, and portability compared to many other forms of energy. With the emergence of newer internal combustion 
engine technologies such as Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) and Reactivity-Controlled Compression 
Ignition (RCCI) engines, understanding the autoignition and heat release chemistry and kinetics of hydrocarbon fuels is 
more important that ever. These new technologies coupled with the emergence of major sources of renewable fuels for 
both gasoline and diesel applications, including butanols and heavier alcohols, bio-diesel, farnesane and high carbon 
number synthetics, further emphasize the need to understand the kinetic effects of blending renewables with 
petroleum derived fuels.
